name: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD)
lead: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a recognised mental health condition in which a person is preoccupied with one or more perceived flaws in their appearance that are minor or not observable to others, to the point that it causes distress or interferes with daily life [1][2]. Because it centres on how people see their own looks, it is directly relevant to anyone working on their appearance: understanding it helps people tell ordinary self-improvement from a cycle of checking, comparing and concealing that can make satisfaction harder to reach.

Clinicians describe repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, comparing with others, camouflaging with clothes or make-up, skin picking and reassurance seeking [1][3]. Evidence-based treatments are cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), often with exposure and response prevention, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs); treatment can reduce symptoms and, according to clinical guidance, many people improve [2][3][4]. Treating the preoccupation can change how a person judges their own face or body, which in turn affects decisions about grooming, fitness and cosmetic procedures.

Online appearance communities discuss BDD frequently, with some members describing their own experience and others debating where the line falls between concern about looks and a disorder [5]. Press and academic coverage of looksmaxxing has raised BDD as a concern, with commentators arguing that rating-focused communities can affect members' wellbeing [26]. BDD was moved into the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group in DSM-5 in 2013 and includes a muscle dysmorphia specifier [1][6].

The International OCD Foundation describes BDD as affecting roughly 1 in 50 people worldwide across genders and backgrounds, and says specialised CBT with exposure and response prevention and SSRI medication are the treatments that respond best [23]. A person who recognises BDD patterns and gets treatment can end up with a steadier self-image and more realistic goals for grooming, fitness and any cosmetic work.

paras: People with BDD worry intensely about a body area, most often the face, skin, hair or nose, and may spend hours a day thinking about it [1][7]. The NHS lists worrying a lot about a specific area, comparing looks with others, checking mirrors a lot or avoiding them, going to great lengths to conceal flaws, and picking at the skin to make it smooth [7].

According to the IOCDF, people with BDD are typically concerned with about five to seven body parts over time, though some focus on one. Commonly named areas include hair, nose, skin, eyes, chin, jaw, neck, face size or shape, and body build, including not feeling muscular enough.[23] Reported behaviours include mirror checking or mirror avoidance, excessive grooming, camouflaging with hats, make-up or posture, reassurance seeking, skin picking, repeated medical or cosmetic appointments, and social avoidance; the IOCDF notes the condition is often hidden because of shame.[23]

Insight varies. Some people recognise that their view may be distorted, while others hold the belief with delusional conviction; about one-third of cases are described as delusional [1]. Depression, social anxiety, OCD and eating disorders often occur alongside BDD [7][1].

Muscle dysmorphia is a subtype in which a person believes their body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite a large or normal build. It can involve excessive exercise, strict diets, wearing layered clothing and, in some cases, use of anabolic steroids [6].

Wikipedia's article describes the concern as usually an overvalued idea rather than a fixed belief, and says BDD is frequently misdiagnosed as social anxiety, OCD, major depression or social phobia and often overlooked by clinicians.[1] It reports social anxiety disorder co-occurring in a wide range (12 to 68.8 percent) of people with BDD, and that the Body Dysmorphic Disorder Questionnaire has been estimated to have high sensitivity and specificity as a screening tool.[1]

A 2016 systematic review estimated weighted prevalence at 1.9% in community adults, 2.2% in adolescents and 3.3% in student populations. Rates were higher in clinical settings: 7.4% in adult and adolescent psychiatric inpatients, 5.8% in adult psychiatric outpatients, 13.2% in general cosmetic surgery, 20.1% in rhinoplasty, 11.2% in orthognathic surgery, 5.2% in orthodontics and cosmetic dentistry, 11.3% in dermatology outpatients, 9.2% in cosmetic dermatology and 11.1% in acne clinics. Women outnumbered men in most settings but not in cosmetic or dermatological ones [8].

A US telephone survey of adults is among the population studies cited, and a 2024 Nature Reviews Disease Primers article says BDD affects about 2% of adults but is underdiagnosed and undertreated [9][2]. A more recent meta-analysis reported a higher pooled estimate, around 17 percent, per Wikipedia [1].

The Wikipedia article notes the pooled figure of about 17 percent comes with regional estimates ranging from 10 percent in Oceania to 31 percent in Latin America, and clinical-sample rates of 24 percent in plastic surgery patients, 18 percent in psychiatric patients and 16 percent in dermatology patients; it also cites higher reported facial dissatisfaction in East Asia.[1] These figures are far above the roughly 2 percent community estimates cited by reviews, which Wikipedia itself presents side by side.[1][2]

Researchers consider causes to be a mix of genetic and environmental influences. A twin-based heritability estimate of 43 percent is cited, along with teasing, bullying and childhood maltreatment as risk factors [1]. The NHS lists family history of BDD, OCD or depression, and past teasing or abuse [7]. A few brain imaging studies suggest differences in regions involved in visual and emotional processing, although firm conclusions cannot yet be drawn [2].
A cognitive-behavioural model of BDD proposes that selective attention to perceived flaws, mental imagery, and safety behaviours such as checking and camouflaging keep the preoccupation going [10].

Wikipedia lists introversion, perfectionism, negative body image, heightened aesthetic sensitivity and childhood abuse or neglect among reported risk factors.[1] Researchers also discuss cultural influences: a 2019 systematic review cited there linked appearance-focused social media use to body image dissatisfaction.[1]

sections.h: Social media, filters and appearance culture
paras: Wikipedia describes 'Snapchat dysmorphia' (also called selfie dysmorphia) as an informal term, credited to British cosmetic surgeon Tijion Esho, for people who seek procedures to resemble filtered or edited images of themselves; it is not a clinical diagnosis.[25] The term was popularised in 2018 alongside a JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery commentary from Boston Medical Center researchers noting that patients were bringing in edited selfies.[25]

A 2019 study cited by Wikipedia found that heavy use of image-focused social media and photo-editing apps was associated with greater openness to cosmetic surgery, and body-image researcher Jasmine Fardouly links negative body image to photo editing. Wikipedia also cautions that many widely quoted statistics come from news outlets, advocacy campaigns or companies rather than peer-reviewed work, and that most research shows associations rather than causation.[25] Researchers recommend that surgeons screen for BDD before operating and discuss realistic goals.[25][1]

In looksmaxxing coverage, Wikipedia's article cites 2024 reporting by the BBC (Farrell, 27 March 2024), The Guardian (Usborne, 15 February 2024) and The Conversation (Rosdahl, 31 January 2024) arguing that communities that rate appearance can contribute to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation among members.[26] A 2025 Sage study (Konig et al.) is cited as advising physicians to help patients distinguish safe beauty practices from harmful ones.[26]

The NHS describes CBT for mild BDD, CBT or an SSRI (most commonly fluoxetine) for moderate cases, and both together for severe cases or when other treatments have not helped. CBT usually includes exposure and response prevention, which involves gradually facing situations that provoke anxiety about appearance; SSRIs can take up to 12 weeks to work and are continued for several months [7].

Trials of psychological treatments include a 1996 pilot randomized trial of a cognitive-behavioural approach, a 2014 randomized trial of modular CBT, a 2022 randomized trial of app-based CBT with coach support, and 2023 randomized trials of cognitive therapy and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy [4][11][12][13][14]. A severity scale based on the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (BDD-YBOCS) was developed in 1997 to rate the disorder [15].

Wikipedia describes Sabine Wilhelm's modular CBT manual, whose elements include psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual prevention, and mindfulness and perceptual retraining, as improving symptoms in trials.[1][11] The IOCDF notes that specialist CBT with exposure and response prevention and SSRI medication are the established treatments, and it maintains a BDD special interest group for professionals, people with lived experience and families.[23][24]

BDD appears in cosmetic settings more than in the general population, as the prevalence figures above show [8]. Reviews and Wikipedia report that cosmetic surgery and non-psychiatric treatments often do not resolve the preoccupation, and that screening of patients is recommended in surgical and dermatology practices [1][16]. A 2025 editorial in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics also addresses BDD in orthodontic care [17].
The NHS page does not give surgical guidance and advises speaking to a GP or mental health specialist before considering surgery [7].

Wikipedia reports that people with BDD often seek dermatology or cosmetic surgery, that these treatments often do not relieve the distress, and that skin picking as self-treatment can cause lesions; it recommends that cosmetic surgeons and psychiatrists work together to screen patients.[1]

Enrico Morselli described 'dysmorphophobia' in 1886; BDD entered the DSM with DSM-III-R in 1987 and moved to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in DSM-5 in 2013 [1]. Muscle dysmorphia was conceptualised in the late 1990s, initially by Pope and colleagues as a reverse form of anorexia, and is now classed as a BDD subtype in DSM-5 and ICD-11 [6].

Wikipedia lists the DSM history as follows: DSM-III (1980) classified it as an atypical somatoform disorder, DSM-III-R (1987) renamed it body dysmorphic disorder, DSM-IV (1994) defined it as preoccupation with an imagined or trivial defect, and DSM-5 (2013) moved it to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum and added the muscle dysmorphia specifier.[1] Sigmund Freud's patient Sergei Pankejeff, the 'Wolf Man', is cited there as showing classic BDD symptoms.[1] The 1997 BDD-YBOCS scale, 1996 pilot CBT trial and later randomized trials mark its growth as a research field.[4][15]

For muscle dysmorphia, a 1993 paper by Pope and colleagues introduced the 'reverse anorexia' idea, and Wikipedia reports that DSM-5 added it as a specifier and ICD-11 lists it as a subtype.[6] Onset is usually between ages 18 and 20; estimates range from 1 to 54 percent of men in studied samples, higher among gym members, weightlifters, bodybuilders and anabolic steroid users; about half have poor or no insight; evidence for treatment is mostly case reports, with CBT, family-based therapy and SSRIs among supported approaches.[6] Media emphasis on muscular physiques since the 1980s is linked in the article to pressure and body comparison.[6]

Reviews report elevated suicidal thoughts in BDD. The IOCDF states that about 66 percent of people with BDD have suicidal thoughts and about 35 percent attempt suicide over a lifetime, and Wikipedia cites one study reporting up to 69 percent with suicidal ideation and notes suicide rates reported at two to twelve times the national average.[23][1] Clinicians treat these figures as a reason for early identification, and the NHS advises seeing a GP or mental health specialist.[7] People in crisis can contact local emergency services or a crisis line in their country.

Prevalence. A systematic review pooled studies across community, psychiatric, cosmetic surgery and dermatology settings and found BDD common in several clinical populations but poorly identified [8]. A 2006 population survey and its 2010 update examined community prevalence [18][19].
Measurement. The 1997 BDD-YBOCS scale was validated in 125 people with BDD [15].

Psychological treatment. A 2014 randomized trial tested modular CBT [11]. A 2022 randomized trial examined app-based CBT with coach support [12]. A 2023 randomized pilot trial compared cognitive therapy for BDD with a wait-list over 12 weeks and followed up outcomes [13]. A 2023 randomized trial of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy measured core symptoms, emotion regulation and executive functioning [14]. A 2023 machine-learning analysis examined predictors of outcome in pharmacotherapy trials [20].
Review articles. A 2024 Nature Reviews Disease Primers paper summarises BDD epidemiology, mechanisms, diagnosis and treatment, stating that CBT and SSRIs are the evidence-based treatments [2].

lore.intro: BDD is a frequent topic on appearance forums, discussed both as a personal experience and as a term that members dispute [5][21].

claims.claim: Looksmaxxer habits are 'a day in the life' and not BDD
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster pasted the NHS symptom list and said it described the average looksmaxxer's daily behaviour, with replies saying almost everyone does these things [5].
claims.experts: Clinical diagnosis requires distress or impairment and repetitive behaviours aimed at checking, correcting or concealing perceived flaws; the NHS notes it can affect work, social life and relationships [2][7].

claims.claim: BDD is 'cope' when a face is objectively unattractive
claims.believers: Some members state that BDD does not apply to people whose faces are actually unattractive.
claims.experts: BDD is defined by preoccupation with flaws that are minor or not observable to others; clinicians also note that appearance concern can occur alongside real features [1][2].

claims.claim: Appearance fixation caused withdrawal from school and work
claims.believers: A poster describes dropping out of school at 17 because of preoccupation with looks and the 'blackpill' [21].
claims.experts: Reviews report that quality of life is markedly impaired across domains in BDD, and treatment with CBT and SSRIs is described as effective [2][7].

claims.claim: Weightlifting can be used to satisfy body image needs, and may become excessive
claims.believers: A T Nation poster described people with BDD turning to the gym to meet their image goals, comparing it to anorexia [22].
claims.experts: Muscle dysmorphia is a recognised BDD subtype, with excessive exercise, strict dieting and sometimes steroid use [6].

claims.claim: Filters and edited selfies are creating a wave of 'Snapchat dysmorphia'
claims.believers: Cosmetic surgeons quoted in coverage say patients now bring filtered images of themselves rather than celebrity photos.[25]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes the term is informal, that research shows associations between photo editing and appearance preoccupation rather than proven causation, and that many circulating statistics are not from peer-reviewed work.[25]

claims.believers: Critics in the BBC, Guardian and Conversation pieces argue that rating culture can harm members' wellbeing.[26]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested whether looksmaxxing community participation causes BDD; the coverage is commentary and journalism, while clinical reviews describe BDD as having genetic and environmental causes.[26][1][2]

claims.claim: Surgery can fix the flaw that causes BDD
claims.believers: People with BDD often seek dermatology or surgical treatment hoping to resolve the preoccupation.[1]
claims.experts: Reviews report that such treatments often do not relieve distress, and screening is recommended; CBT and SSRIs are the established treatments.[1][2][16]

card.summary: A recognised psychiatric disorder of fixation on perceived flaws, treated with CBT and SSRIs.
card.note: High suicidal ideation reported; professional mental health support is recommended by clinicians.

quick.overview:
BDD is a clinical disorder in which a person is consumed by a perceived appearance flaw that others barely notice or cannot see.

It affects roughly 2 percent of people by community estimates and is more common in cosmetic and dermatology settings.
quick.mechanism: Researchers describe a biopsychosocial origin, with checking and avoidance rituals that maintain the preoccupation.
quick.risks: Reviews report high rates of suicidal ideation, and cosmetic procedures rarely relieve the distress. CBT and SSRIs are the recommended treatments.

chain: CBT or SSRI treatment reduces the preoccupation
More accurate self-image and more informed choices about grooming and procedures
angle.text: BDD describes a pattern where perceived flaws dominate attention. People who recognise the pattern can use CBT-based approaches and clinical care so that their efforts to improve looks, from skincare to surgery consultations, are based on how they actually look and on realistic goals.
